story.en: Uber HQ, Friday evening. Product manager Sneha walks in: "We need top earning drivers per city for bonus distribution." Time to combine trips and drivers data.
story.ta: Uber HQ, Friday evening. Product manager Sneha vandhu sonnaanga: "City-wise top earning drivers venum — bonus kudukanum." Trips-um drivers-um join panna time.
story.hi: Uber HQ, Friday shaam. Product manager Sneha bolti hai: "Har city ke top earning drivers chahiye — bonus dena hai." Trips aur drivers ko join karna padega.
story.te: Uber HQ, Friday evening. Product manager Sneha cheppindi: "City-wise top earning drivers kavali — bonus ivvali." Trips mariyu drivers ni join cheyyali.

question.en: Find total earnings of each driver and show top 3 earning drivers per city.
question.ta: Oru driver evlo total earn pannirukkaan nu calculate panni, city-ku top 3 earning drivers kaatu.
question.hi: Har driver ka total earning nikalo aur har city ke top 3 drivers dikhao.
question.te: Prathi driver total earnings calculate chesi, prathi city lo top 3 drivers chupinchu.

title.hi: Drivers aur trips ko join karo
title.te: Drivers mariyu trips ni join cheyyali

en: The drivers table has name and city — but no fare. The trips table has fare amounts — but no city or driver name. The only link between them is driver_id.
JOIN finds matching rows in both tables using the condition d.driver_id = t.driver_id. Every trip row gets paired with the correct driver row.
We use aliases: d for drivers, t for trips. This shortens the query and avoids repeating full table names every time.
Without JOIN, you'd have to run two separate queries and manually match rows by driver_id — JOIN does this automatically in one shot.
The result of this step: each row now has driver_id, driver_name, city, and fare together in one place — ready for the next aggregation step.
ta: drivers table-la driver peru, city irukku — aaana fare illai. trips table-la fare irukku — aaana city, driver peru theriyaadhu. Rendu tables-um driver_id-la mattum connect aaguthu.
JOIN panna, d.driver_id = t.driver_id match aana oda rendu tables-oda rows combine aagum. Oru driver-oda ella trips-um avan row-oda join aagum.
d nu drivers-ku alias, t nu trips-ku alias. Ithunala query short-a irukum, oru table peru repeat panna thaevaillai.
JOIN panna marandha, neenga rendu separate queries poda vendum, manually driver_id match panna try panum — JOIN ithay automatically oru query-la panniduthey.
Indha step-oda result: oru row-la driver_id, driver_name, city, fare ellam onra varum — next step-ku ready.
hi: drivers table mein naam aur city hai — lekin fare nahi. trips table mein fare hai — lekin city ya driver naam nahi. Dono tables sirf driver_id se connected hain.
JOIN karte waqt, jahan d.driver_id = t.driver_id match karta hai, wahan dono tables ki rows ek saath combine ho jaati hain. Har trip apne sahi driver ke saath pair ho jaata hai.
d drivers ka alias hai, t trips ka alias hai. Isse query chhoti rehti hai aur baar baar poora table naam likhna nahi padta.
JOIN nahi kiya toh do alag queries chalani padti aur manually driver_id se match karna padta — JOIN yeh kaam ek hi query mein automatically karta hai.
Is step ka result: ab ek row mein driver_id, driver_name, city, aur fare — sab ek jagah aa gaye. Agle step ke liye taiyaar.
te: drivers table lo driver peru, city undi — kaani fare ledu. trips table lo fare undi — kaani city, driver peru ledu. Rendu tables ni connect cheyyedhi driver_id matrame.
JOIN chesina tarvata, d.driver_id = t.driver_id match ayyina chota rendu tables rows combine avutaayi. Prathi trip correct driver row tho pair avutundi.
d ante drivers alias, t ante trips alias. Daantalla query chinna ga untundi, prathi sariki full table peru rayyakkarledu.
JOIN cheyyakapoina, rendu separate queries run cheyyali, manually driver_id match cheyyali — JOIN idi oka query lo automatic ga chestundi.
Ee step result: oka row lo driver_id, driver_name, city, fare anni oka saari vastunayi — next step ki ready.

title.hi: Driver ke hisaab se total earnings nikalo

steps.sql:
SELECT d.driver_id,
       d.driver_name,
       d.city,
       SUM(t.fare) AS total_earnings
FROM drivers d
JOIN trips t ON d.driver_id = t.driver_id
GROUP BY d.driver_id, d.driver_name, d.city
ORDER BY total_earnings DESC;

en: SUM(t.fare) adds up all fare values for each driver across all their trips. For example, driver D001 has 3 trips: 250.50 + 180.00 + 320.75 = 751.25 total.
GROUP BY d.driver_id, d.driver_name, d.city tells SQL: group all rows with the same driver_id together, then calculate SUM separately for each group.
Why include driver_name and city in GROUP BY? SQL rule: every column in SELECT that is NOT inside an aggregate function (like SUM) must also appear in GROUP BY.
AS total_earnings gives a clean, readable name to the calculated column. Without it, the output column header would literally say SUM(t.fare) — confusing.
ORDER BY total_earnings DESC sorts results from highest earner to lowest. This makes it easy to spot the top drivers at a glance.
At this point you have one row per driver with their total earnings — but you still cannot filter top 3 per city. For that, you need ranking logic in the next step.
ta: SUM(t.fare) oru driver-oda ella trips-oda fare-a add pannum. Example: D001-ku 3 trips irukku — 250.50 + 180.00 + 320.75 = 751.25 total.
GROUP BY d.driver_id, d.driver_name, d.city — SQL-ku solluchu: same driver_id-oda ella rows-a oru group-a potu, prathi group-ku alag SUM calculate pannu.
Yen driver_name-um city-um GROUP BY-la varuthu? SQL rule: SELECT-la aggregate function (SUM) inside illatha ella column-um GROUP BY-la varanumnu mandatory.
AS total_earnings — calculated column-ku oru clean name kudukuthu. Illana output header literally 'SUM(t.fare)' nu varum — confusing-a irukum.
ORDER BY total_earnings DESC — highest earner mudhal, lowest last. Oru paarthale yaar top driver nu theriyum.
Ippo oru driver-ku oru row irukku total earnings-oda — aaana city-wise top 3 filter panna innum oru step venum. Adhu next-la.
hi: SUM(t.fare) ek driver ke saare trips ke fares jod deta hai. Example: D001 ke 3 trips hain — 250.50 + 180.00 + 320.75 = 751.25 total.
GROUP BY d.driver_id, d.driver_name, d.city — SQL ko bolta hai: same driver_id wali saari rows ko ek group mein daalo, phir har group ke liye alag SUM nikalo.
driver_name aur city GROUP BY mein kyun? SQL ka rule: SELECT mein jo column kisi aggregate function (jaise SUM) ke andar nahi hai, woh GROUP BY mein bhi hona chahiye.
AS total_earnings — calculated column ko ek samajhne wala naam deta hai. Warna output header literally 'SUM(t.fare)' dikhega — confusing lagega.
ORDER BY total_earnings DESC — sabse zyada kamaane wala pehle, sabse kum wala last. Ek nazar mein top drivers dikh jaate hain.
Ab har driver ki ek row hai total earnings ke saath — lekin abhi bhi har city ke top 3 filter nahi kar sakte. Uske liye ranking logic chahiye — woh agla step hai.
te: SUM(t.fare) oka driver anni trips fares ni add chestundi. Example: D001 ki 3 trips unnaayi — 250.50 + 180.00 + 320.75 = 751.25 total.
GROUP BY d.driver_id, d.driver_name, d.city — SQL ki cheppistundi: same driver_id unna anni rows ni oka group lo petto, prathi group ki alagugaa SUM calculate cheyyali.
driver_name mariyu city kuda GROUP BY lo endhuku? SQL rule: SELECT lo unna column edi aggregate function (SUM) lota lekapoina, adi GROUP BY lo kuda undaali — mandatory.
AS total_earnings — calculated column ki clean name isthundi. Lekapoina output header literally 'SUM(t.fare)' ani kanipistundi — confusing ga untundi.
ORDER BY total_earnings DESC — highest earner mundu, lowest last. Oka chupulo top drivers ardam avutundi.
Ipudu prathi driver ki oka row total earnings tho undi — kaani city-wise top 3 filter cheyyataniki inko step kavali. Adhi tarvata lo unnadi.

title.en: Get top 3 drivers per city using ROW_NUMBER
title.ta: ROW_NUMBER use panni city-ku top 3 drivers kaatu
title.hi: ROW_NUMBER se har city ke top 3 drivers nikalo
title.te: ROW_NUMBER use chesi prathi city lo top 3 drivers kanugonu

steps.sql:
SELECT driver_id, driver_name, city, total_earnings
FROM (
  SELECT d.driver_id,
         d.driver_name,
         d.city,
         SUM(t.fare) AS total_earnings,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY d.city
           ORDER BY SUM(t.fare) DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM drivers d
  JOIN trips t ON d.driver_id = t.driver_id
  GROUP BY d.driver_id, d.driver_name, d.city
) ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;

en: The previous step gave total earnings per driver — but we need top 3 per city, not overall top 3. For that, we must rank drivers within each city separately.
ROW_NUMBER() is a window function. Unlike GROUP BY which collapses multiple rows into one, window functions add a new column to existing rows without removing any rows.
OVER (...) defines the 'window' — the rules for how ROW_NUMBER should group and sort. Think of OVER as: 'apply this ranking logic inside this specific window of rows'.
PARTITION BY d.city splits drivers into groups by city before ranking. Chennai drivers get ranked among themselves. Delhi drivers get ranked among themselves. Each city is independent.
ORDER BY SUM(t.fare) DESC inside OVER means: within each city group, assign rank 1 to the highest earner, rank 2 to the second highest, rank 3 to third, and so on.
The inner query is wrapped in a subquery (aliased as 'ranked') because SQL evaluates WHERE before window functions. You cannot write WHERE rn <= 3 in the same query — it must be in an outer query.
WHERE rn <= 3 in the outer query keeps only rows where the rank is 1, 2, or 3 — meaning the top 3 earners from each city partition.
Why not just use LIMIT 3? LIMIT 3 would give the top 3 drivers globally across all cities. ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY is the correct approach when you need top-N within each group.
ta: Previous step-la driver-wise total kitechu — aaana overall top 3 illai, city-ku top 3 venum. Adhanala prathi city-la separately rank kodukanum.
ROW_NUMBER() oru window function. GROUP BY rows-a collapse pannum (merge pannum) — aaana window functions existing rows-la oru new column mattum add pannum, rows pogaadhu.
OVER (...) 'window'-a define pannum — ROW_NUMBER-ku how to group, how to sort nu solluchu. 'Indha window-la indha ranking logic apply pannu' nu think pannu.
PARTITION BY d.city — rank kudukka munnaadi drivers-a city-wise split pannum. Chennai drivers Chennai-la rank aaguvaaanga, Delhi drivers Delhi-la — prathi city independent.
OVER-la ORDER BY SUM(t.fare) DESC — prathi city-la highest earner-ku rank 1, next-ku rank 2, ippadi continue aagum.

Inner query-a subquery-la (ranked nu alias) wrap panna karanam — SQL WHERE-a window functions-ku munnaadi evaluate pannum. Athey query-la WHERE rn <= 3 elutha mudiyaadhu — outer query-la mattum elutha mudiyum.
Outer query-la WHERE rn <= 3 — rn 1, 2, 3 ulla rows mattum varum, meaning prathi city-la top 3 earners mattum output-la varum.
Yen LIMIT 3 use panna koodaadhu? LIMIT 3 overall global top 3 kudukum — city-wise illai. Per-city top-N-ku ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY dhaan sari aana way.
hi: Pichle step mein driver-wise total mila — lekin overall top 3 nahi, har city ke top 3 chahiye. Isliye har city ke andar drivers ko alag se rank dena hoga.
ROW_NUMBER() ek window function hai. GROUP BY rows ko collapse (merge) kar deta hai — lekin window functions existing rows mein sirf ek naya column add karte hain, rows nahi hatate.
OVER (...) 'window' define karta hai — ROW_NUMBER ko batata hai ki kaise group aur sort karna hai. Sochiye: 'is window ke andar yeh ranking logic lagao'.
PARTITION BY d.city — rank dene se pehle drivers ko city ke hisaab se group karta hai. Chennai ke drivers apas mein rank hote hain, Delhi ke apas mein — har city independent hai.
OVER ke andar ORDER BY SUM(t.fare) DESC — har city ke group mein highest earner ko rank 1, usse kam wale ko rank 2, aur aage aise.

Inner query ko subquery (alias: ranked) mein wrap karna padta hai kyunki SQL WHERE clause ko window functions se pehle process karta hai. Usi query mein WHERE rn <= 3 nahi likh sakte — yeh bahar wali query mein likhna zaroori hai.
Outer query mein WHERE rn <= 3 — sirf woh rows rakhta hai jahan rank 1, 2, ya 3 hai, yani har city ke top 3 earners hi output mein aate hain.
LIMIT 3 kyun nahi chalega? LIMIT 3 globally sabse upar ke 3 drivers dega — city-wise nahi. Har group mein top-N chahiye toh ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY hi sahi tarika hai.
te: Mundu step lo driver-wise total vasindi — kaani overall top 3 kaadu, prathi city ki top 3 kavali. Kaabatti prathi city lo drivers ni separately rank cheyyaali.
ROW_NUMBER() oka window function. GROUP BY rows ni collapse (merge) chestundi — kaani window functions existing rows lo oka new column matrame add chestaayi, rows teyyavu.
OVER (...) 'window' ni define chestundi — ROW_NUMBER ki ela group cheyyaalo, ela sort cheyyaalo cheppistundi. 'Ee window lo ee ranking logic apply cheyyali' ani alochinchu.
PARTITION BY d.city — rank ivvataniki mundu drivers ni city wise split chestundi. Chennai drivers Chennai lo rank avutaaru, Delhi drivers Delhi lo — prathi city independent.
OVER lo ORDER BY SUM(t.fare) DESC — prathi city group lo highest earner ki rank 1, tarvata rank 2, ila continue avutundi.
Inner query ni subquery (alias: ranked) lo wrap cheyyali, endukante SQL WHERE ni window functions kanna mundu process chestundi. Aye query lo WHERE rn <= 3 rayyaledu — baita query lo rayyali.
Outer query lo WHERE rn <= 3 — rank 1, 2, 3 unna rows matrame filter avutaayi, ante prathi city top 3 earners matrame output lo vastunayi.
LIMIT 3 endhuku pani cheyyadu? LIMIT 3 globally top 3 isthundi — city-wise kaadu. Prathi group lo top-N kavali ante ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY e correct approach.

story.en: Wednesday morning at Uber's Rider Experience team. A few trips in the system have no fare recorded at all — the ride ended before the fare could be calculated, maybe from an app crash or a cancelled payment. The team wants each rider's average fare per trip, but those fare-less trips still happened and still used a driver's time, so they shouldn't just be dropped from the average — they need to count as zero, not disappear.
story.ta: Wednesday morning Uber oda Rider Experience team la. System la konjum trips ku fare record aagala, app crash alladhu cancelled payment nala fare calculate aaguradhukku munnadi ride mudinjidichu. Team ku ovvoru rider oda average fare per trip venum, aana andha fare illaadha trips nadandhurukku, driver oda time um use pannirukku, so avanga a average la irundhu drop pannakoodadhu, avanga zero nu count aagananum, disappear aagakoodadhu.
story.hi: Wednesday morning Uber ke Rider Experience team mein. System mein kuch trips ka fare bilkul record nahi hua — app crash ya cancelled payment ki wajah se fare calculate hone se pehle hi ride khatam ho gayi. Team ko har rider ka average fare per trip chahiye, lekin wo fare-less trips actually hui thi aur driver ka time bhi use hua tha, isliye unhe average se hata dena sahi nahi — unhe zero maan ke count karna hai, gayab nahi karna.
story.te: Wednesday morning Uber Rider Experience team lo. System lo konni trips ki fare ye record avvaledu, app crash leda cancelled payment valla fare calculate avvakamunde ride mugisindi. Team ki prathi rider average fare per trip kavali, kaani aa fare leni trips nijamga jarigayi, driver time kuda vadabadindi, so vaatini average nunchi teeseyakudadu, vaatini zero ga count cheyali, maripoyela kaadu.

question.en: For each rider, calculate the total number of trips they've taken and their average fare per trip. Treat any trip with a missing (NULL) fare_amount as 0 when calculating the average, rather than excluding it. Return rider_name, total_trips, and avg_fare (rounded to 2 decimal places), sorted by avg_fare in descending order.
question.ta: Ovvoru rider kum, avanga edutha total trips count matrum avanga oda average fare per trip a calculate pannunga. Edhavadhu trip oda fare_amount NULL a irundha, average calculate pannumbodhu adha exclude pannama 0 nu treat pannunga. rider_name, total_trips, matrum avg_fare a (two decimal places ku round panni) return pannunga, avg_fare descending order la sort pannunga.
question.hi: Har rider ke liye, unki total trips count aur unka average fare per trip calculate karo. Agar kisi trip ka fare_amount NULL hai, toh average nikaalte waqt use exclude karne ke bajaye 0 maano. rider_name, total_trips, aur avg_fare (do decimal places tak round karke) return karo, avg_fare ke descending order mein sort karke.
question.te: Prathi rider ki, vaalla theesukunna total trips count mariyu vaalla average fare per trip ni calculate cheyandi. edaina trip fare_amount NULL unte, average calculate chese appudu daanini exclude cheyakunda 0 ga treat cheyandi. rider_name, total_trips, mariyu avg_fare ni (rendu decimal places ki round chesi) return cheyandi, avg_fare descending order lo sort chesi.

title.en: Calculate total trips and average fare per rider
title.ta: Ovvoru rider kum total trips matrum average fare calculate pannunga
title.hi: Har rider ke total trips aur average fare calculate karo
title.te: Prathi rider ki total trips mariyu average fare calculate cheyandi

steps.sql:
SELECT r.rider_name,
       COUNT(t.trip_id) AS total_trips,
       AVG(t.fare_amount) AS avg_fare
FROM riders r
JOIN rider_trips t ON t.rider_id = r.rider_id
GROUP BY r.rider_id, r.rider_name
ORDER BY r.rider_name;

en: riders and rider_trips are joined on rider_id so each trip can be attributed to the rider who took it. JOIN naturally drops nothing here, since every trip has a valid rider_id — the missing data problem in this question is the fare, not the relationship between the two tables.

COUNT(t.trip_id) counts trips using the trip_id column specifically, not fare_amount or a bare COUNT(*) — trip_id is never NULL, so every trip a rider took is counted correctly, including the ones with no recorded fare.

AVG(t.fare_amount) computes the average directly on the raw fare column. SQL's AVG() ignores NULL values entirely — both from the sum and from the count it divides by — so a rider with one NULL-fare trip out of three gets averaged over the two priced trips only, not all three.
Look at Priya Desai: her average here is 475, computed from just two priced trips (500 and 450), with her third trip — the one with no fare — silently excluded from the calculation entirely.
ta: riders matrum rider_trips rider_id vachi join pannirukku, so ovvoru trip um adha edukkura rider ku attribute aagum. Ella trip kum valid rider_id irukkura, so JOIN edhuvum drop pannaadhu, indha question la missing data problem fare la irukku, rendu table oda relationship la illa.

COUNT(t.trip_id) trip_id column vachi trips a count pannum, fare_amount alladhu bare COUNT(*) illa, trip_id oru pothum NULL a irukkadhu, so oru rider edukkura ella trip um correct a count aagum, fare record aagama irukkura trips serndhu.

AVG(t.fare_amount) raw fare column la direct a average calculate pannum. SQL oda AVG() NULL values a completely ignore pannum, sum la irundhum, adha divide pannura count lla irundhum, so moonu trip la oru NULL fare trip irukkura rider, rendu priced trips mattum vachi average pannappadum, moonu trip um illa.

Priya Desai a paarunga: ivangaloda average inge 475, rendu priced trips mattum vachi calculate aagirukku (500 matrum 450), moonaavadhu trip, fare illama irukkura adhu, calculation la irundhu completely exclude aagirukku.
hi: riders aur rider_trips ko rider_id par join kiya gaya hai, taaki har trip us rider ko attribute ho sake jisne wo trip li thi. Yahan JOIN kuch bhi drop nahi karta, kyunki har trip ka rider_id valid hai — is question mein missing data ki problem fare mein hai, dono tables ke relationship mein nahi.

COUNT(t.trip_id) trip_id column use karke trips count karta hai, fare_amount ya bare COUNT(*) nahi — trip_id kabhi NULL nahi hota, isliye rider ki har trip sahi se count hoti hai, un trips samet jinka fare record nahi hua.

AVG(t.fare_amount) raw fare column par seedha average calculate karta hai. SQL ka AVG() NULL values ko poori tarah ignore karta hai — sum se bhi aur jis count se divide karta hai usse bhi — isliye teen trips mein se ek NULL-fare trip wale rider ka average sirf do priced trips par calculate hota hai, teeno par nahi.
Priya Desai ko dekho: unka average yahan 475 hai, sirf do priced trips (500 aur 450) se calculate hua, unki teesri trip — jiska fare nahi tha — calculation se poori tarah bahar reh gayi.
te: riders mariyu rider_trips rider_id meeda join chesaru, so prathi trip aa trip theesukunna rider ki attribute avutundi. Ikkada JOIN emi drop cheyadu, endukante prathi trip ki valid rider_id undi, ee question lo missing data problem fare lo undi, rendu tables relationship lo kaadu.

COUNT(t.trip_id) trip_id column vaadi trips ni count chestundi, fare_amount leda bare COUNT(*) kaadu, trip_id eppudu NULL kaadu, so oka rider theesukunna prathi trip correct ga count avutundi, fare record avvani trips tho saha.

AVG(t.fare_amount) raw fare column meeda neruga average calculate chestundi. SQL AVG() NULL values ni poorthiga ignore chestundi, sum nunchi kuda, daanini divide chese count nunchi kuda, so mudu trips lo oka NULL fare trip unna rider average kevalam rendu priced trips meeda calculate avutundi, mudintilo kaadu.
Priya Desai ni chudandi: aame average ikkada 475, rendu priced trips (500 mariyu 450) nunchi calculate ayyindi, aame mudo trip, fare leni adi, calculation nunchi poorthiga bayata migilipoyindi.

title.en: Fix the average with COALESCE so missing fares count as zero
title.ta: COALESCE vachi average a fix pannunga, missing fares zero nu count aagum
title.hi: COALESCE se average theek karo, taaki missing fares zero maani jaayein
title.te: COALESCE tho average ni fix cheyandi, missing fares zero ga count avvali

steps.sql:
SELECT r.rider_name,
       COUNT(t.trip_id) AS total_trips,
       AVG(COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0)) AS avg_fare
FROM riders r
JOIN rider_trips t ON t.rider_id = r.rider_id
GROUP BY r.rider_id, r.rider_name
ORDER BY r.rider_name;

en: The only change from the previous step is wrapping fare_amount in COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0) inside the AVG — everything else about the query, including which rows are counted, stays the same.

COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0) replaces a NULL fare with 0 before AVG ever sees it. A trip with no recorded fare now genuinely participates in the average as a zero-value trip, instead of being invisible to the calculation.

This changes the denominator's effective weight, not just which values get summed: for a rider with one NULL-fare trip out of three, the average now divides by all three trips' worth of value (two fares plus one zero), not just the two priced ones.

Priya Desai's average drops from 475 to about 316.67 — same three trips, same two real fares, but now her fare-less trip pulls the average down instead of being erased from it. Kiran Rao's average is cut in half, from 90 to 45, for the same reason.
ta: Munnaadi step la irundhu maatram, AVG kulla fare_amount a COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0) vachi wrap pannradhu mattum thaan, query oda mattha ella um, edhu rows count aaguthu nu adhu ulpada, adhe madhiri irukku.

COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0) AVG paakkura munnaadiye NULL fare a 0 nu replace pannidum. Fare record aagama irukkura trip ippo genuinely zero value trip a average la participate pannum, calculation ku invisible a irukkuradhukku pathila.

Idhu sum aagura values mattum illa, denominator oda effective weight a maathidum: moonu trip la oru NULL fare trip irukkura rider kku, average ippo moonu trip oda mudhal value a divide pannum (rendu fares plus oru zero), rendu priced trips mattum illa.

Priya Desai oda average 475 la irundhu 316.67 varaikkum kammi aaguthu, adhe moonu trips, adhe rendu real fares, aana ippo avangaloda fare illaadha trip average a kammi pannuthu, adhula irundhu erase aagama. Kiran Rao oda average um adhe karanam ku paadhi aaguthu, 90 la irundhu 45.
hi: Pichle step se sirf itna change hua hai: AVG ke andar fare_amount ko COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0) mein wrap kar diya gaya hai — query ka baaki sab kuch, kaunse rows count ho rahe hain samet, wahi hai.

COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0) NULL fare ko 0 se replace kar deta hai, isse pehle ki AVG use dekhe. Jis trip ka fare record nahi hua, wo ab average mein genuinely zero-value trip ke roop mein shaamil hoti hai, calculation ke liye invisible hone ke bajaye.

Yeh sirf yeh nahi badalta ki kaunse values jodi ja rahi hain, balki denominator ka effective weight bhi badalta hai: teen trips mein se ek NULL-fare trip wale rider ke liye, average ab teeno trips ki value se divide hota hai (do fares plus ek zero), sirf do priced trips se nahi.

Priya Desai ka average 475 se ghatkar lagbhag 316.67 ho jaata hai — wahi teen trips, wahi do asli fares, lekin ab unki fare-less trip average ko neeche khinchti hai, usse mit jaane ke bajaye. Kiran Rao ka average bhi isi wajah se aadha ho jaata hai, 90 se 45.
te: Previous step nunchi matrame change ayindi enti ante AVG lopala fare_amount ni COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0) tho wrap cheyadam, query lo migilina anni, e rows count avutunnayo saha, ade la undi.

COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0) AVG chudakamunde NULL fare ni 0 tho replace chestundi. Fare record avvani trip ippudu genuinely zero value trip ga average lo participate chestundi, calculation ki invisible ga undakunda.

Idi e values sum avutunnayo matrame kaadu, denominator effective weight ni kuda marustundi: mudu trips lo oka NULL fare trip unna rider ki, average ippudu mudu trips viluva tho divide avutundi, rendu fares plus oka zero, rendu priced trips tho kaadu.

Priya Desai average 475 nunchi 316.67 ki thaggutundi, ade mudu trips, ade rendu real fares, kaani ippudu aame fare leni trip average ni takkuva chestundi, danilo nunchi erase avvakunda. Kiran Rao average kuda ade karananiki sagam avutundi, 90 nunchi 45 ki.

title.hi: Final query — clean output ke saath

steps.sql:
SELECT r.rider_name,
       COUNT(t.trip_id) AS total_trips,
       ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(t.fare_amount, 0)), 2) AS avg_fare
FROM riders r
JOIN rider_trips t ON t.rider_id = r.rider_id
GROUP BY r.rider_id, r.rider_name
ORDER BY avg_fare DESC;

en: ROUND(..., 2) rounds the average to two decimal places — AVG on a REAL column can return long trailing decimals (223.333333...) even when the underlying data is clean money values.
ORDER BY avg_fare DESC sorts the final output by the corrected average, highest first — this is a plain ORDER BY on the outer query, separate from anything inside the aggregate functions.

Notice the ranking itself changes between the naive and corrected versions, not just the numbers: Priya Desai was highest in step 1 (475) but drops to second place here (316.67), behind Divya Menon, once her fare-less trip is counted instead of ignored.

This is the complete answer: every rider who has taken at least one trip, with their true trip count and an average fare that accounts for every trip they took — including the ones that ended without a fare on record.
